theme: I will give thanks; God judges the world in righteousness
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 9 slowly, twice. This is a longer Psalm, twenty verses, but it moves quickly. As you read, notice how the Psalm alternates between thanksgiving for God’s past faithfulness and prayer about God’s future judgment. It is a fitting Psalm to close out the meditations of Unit 2.
settingTheScene:
We are at the end of Unit 2. We have walked through the spread of sin in the post-flood world, the catastrophe of the flood itself, the Noahic Covenant of preservation, and the pride and scattering of Babel. Throughout, we have seen a particular pattern: human evil is real, judgment is real, but God’s faithfulness to preserve his people and his world is also real. Today’s psalm gathers up many of these threads in worship.

Psalm 9 is attributed to David, sung “to the tune of Muth-labben,” the meaning of which is uncertain. The psalm celebrates God’s righteous judgment of the nations and his vindication of the oppressed. It is the perfect Old Testament prayer for those who have just been reading about humanity in rebellion.
observation: The psalm opens with whole-hearted thanksgiving: “I will give thanks to the LORD with my whole heart; I will recount all of your wonderful deeds.”
Verses 4-6 describe past acts of divine judgment: God has rebuked the nations, the wicked have perished, their cities have been overthrown.
Verse 7 is theological: “The LORD sits enthroned forever; he has established his throne for justice.” Justice is built into the throne itself.
Verse 8: “He judges the world with righteousness; he judges the peoples with uprightness.” Universal scope, all nations, with perfect justice.
Verse 9: “The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble.” Justice for the wicked is mercy for the oppressed.
Verse 10: “Those who know your name put their trust in you, for you, O LORD, have not forsaken those who seek you.” Knowing God’s name leads to trust.
Verses 11-12 are about declaring God’s deeds to the nations, taking the message outward.
Verses 15-16: The wicked are caught in the nets they set for others. Justice is poetic, sin returns on itself.
Verse 17: “The wicked shall return to Sheol, all the nations that forget God.” Forgetting God has eschatological consequences.
Verse 18 is the great hinge: “For the needy shall not always be forgotten, and the hope of the poor shall not perish forever.”
The psalm closes with a prayer for God to arise and judge, “Let the nations know that they are but men.”
interpretation:
Psalm 9 is a song about the justice of God, sung by someone who has seen enough of human wickedness to want it. It is honest about evil and confident about God’s response. It is exactly the right psalm after Unit 2.

The psalm opens with thanksgiving, but notice what David is thankful for. He is thankful for God’s “wonderful deeds.” And as you read on, those wonderful deeds include God’s acts of judgment against the wicked. This sets a tone that may feel strange to modern ears. We tend to be uncomfortable with celebrating divine judgment. But the psalmist is not uncomfortable. To him, God’s judgment of the wicked is something worth singing about, because it means the oppressed are vindicated, the world is being put right, and the king of justice is on his throne.

Verse 7 captures the heart of the psalm’s theology: “The LORD sits enthroned forever; he has established his throne for justice.” Justice is not a peripheral concern for God. It is built into the foundation of his kingship. He does not occasionally judge; he reigns from a throne whose central purpose is judgment. And the next verse expands the scope: “He judges the world with righteousness; he judges the peoples with uprightness.” This is universal. Every nation. Every person. All judged by God’s perfect standard, in his perfect time.

But here is where the psalm reframes everything. The judgment of the wicked is the salvation of the oppressed. Verse 9: “The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble.” The same God who is terrifying to the proud is a refuge for the broken. The same justice that frightens the comfortable is good news for the abused, the forgotten, the powerless. If you are tempted to wish God were less just, ask yourself what you are wishing for. A God who does not judge is a God who does not care about the oppressed. A God who never punishes is a God who never vindicates. The justice of God is the hope of the poor.

Verse 10 introduces a tender phrase: “Those who know your name put their trust in you.” Knowing God’s name is biblical shorthand for knowing God personally. To know his name is to know who he really is, his character, his promises, his commitments. And to know him is to trust him. People do not trust strangers. They trust people they know. The reason some people do not trust God is that they do not yet know him. The reason believers can trust him even in dark times is that they have come to know his name.

Then comes the great social vision of the psalm in verses 11-12 and 16-18. The God who judges remembers the blood of the oppressed. He does not forget the cry of the afflicted. The needy will not always be forgotten. The hope of the poor will not perish forever. These verses are the seedbed of the entire prophetic tradition in the Old Testament, where the prophets thunder against injustice on God’s behalf. They are also the foundation of the church’s commitment to the poor and the oppressed. The God we worship is the God who hears the cry of the needy.

There is also a fascinating image of poetic justice in verses 15-16. “The nations have sunk in the pit that they made; in the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught. The LORD has made himself known; he has executed judgment; the wicked are snared in the work of their own hands.” Evil has a way of consuming those who practice it. The traps set for others entangle their setters. The systems built to oppress eventually collapse on those who built them. This is not karma in an impersonal sense; it is the moral grain of the universe set by God. Sin destroys those who indulge it. The wicked are not so much punished by God as left to be destroyed by their own choices.

The psalm closes with a prayer: “Arise, O LORD! Let not man prevail; let the nations be judged before you! Put them in fear, O LORD! Let the nations know that they are but men!” This is a strong prayer, and it should feel strong in our mouths. It is a prayer for God to be God, for him to step in, judge the nations, and remind them of their creatureliness. After reading about Babel, this prayer feels exactly right. The nations have forgotten that they are but men. We pray that God will remind them.
connection: Unit 2 has shown us human sin at every scale, individual (Cain), familial (Noah’s drunkenness), civilizational (Babel). Psalm 9 is the appropriate prayer in response. We have seen the wicked, and we cry out for justice. We have seen God’s preservation through covenant, and we give thanks. We have seen the oppressed of every era, those crushed by Lamechs and Nimrods, and we trust that God will not forget them. The psalm anticipates everything Unit 3 will develop: God arises, the nations are judged, and one man (Abram) is called to be the beginning of God’s plan to bless the very nations that have rebelled against him.
application:
Today, let this Psalm shape three things in you.

First, your view of God’s justice. Many modern Christians have unconsciously absorbed the idea that God’s judgment is embarrassing or harsh, something to apologize for. The psalmist shows us a different posture. Divine justice is something to thank God for. It is the foundation of his throne. It is the hope of the oppressed. If you struggle with the doctrine of God’s wrath, read this Psalm and ask why the people of God have sung it joyfully for three thousand years. The answer is that they knew what we sometimes forget: justice is mercy when it is directed at oppression.

Second, your view of God’s care for the oppressed. The God of Psalm 9 hears the cry of the afflicted. He does not forget the blood of the oppressed. The needy shall not always be forgotten. This commits the believer to active concern for those who suffer in this world. If God remembers the oppressed, his people cannot pretend not to see them. Today, ask yourself: who in your life is being forgotten? In your church, your neighborhood, your city, your family? The God you worship sees them. Let your eyes see them too.

Third, your view of your own situation. If you are facing injustice today, at work, in your family, in your community, Psalm 9 is your prayer. The LORD is a stronghold for the oppressed. He has not forsaken those who seek him. The traps set for you will, in God’s time, fall on the heads of those who set them. You do not have to retaliate, because justice is not your job. Justice is God’s throne. Trust him. Wait for him. Sing his praise. And know that the same God who judged Babel will, in his time, vindicate every faithful sufferer.
prayerPrompts: Give thanks to God with your whole heart, naming something he has done.
Ask him to help you trust him more fully as you know him better.
Pray for someone who is poor or oppressed, and ask what he might have you do.
